analyses.title: Time to Split: Exploring Data Splitting Strategies for Offline Evaluation of Sequential Recommenders
analyses.research_question: How do leave-one-out and alternative global temporal splitting, target-selection, and validation strategies affect realism, metric consistency, model ranking, and model selection in offline evaluation of sequential recommender systems?
analyses.methodology: The authors formalized leave-one-out (LOO) and several global temporal split (GTS) variants, including All, First, Last, Random, and Successive target selection, together with global-temporal, last-training-item, and user-based validation schemes. They evaluated the protocols on eight real-world sequential recommendation datasets using established sequential recommender baselines and, for ranking analysis, a non-neural sequential kNN baseline. Evaluation used unsampled HR@K, MRR@K, and NDCG@K at several K values, subset and temporal-gap statistics, Kendall and Spearman correlations, model-rank comparisons, and experiments with retraining on combined training and validation data.

key_findings.finding: LOO can violate the global interaction timeline and was less aligned with the temporally separated Successive evaluation than several GTS alternatives, while changes in split and target definition could materially change model rankings.
GTS Random had the strongest average agreement with GTS Successive, while GTS Last also showed high agreement and offered a deterministic, lower-cost alternative to Successive evaluation.

GTS All showed especially poor agreement with Successive evaluation because its set-valued target does not match standard next-item prediction, and GTS First was weakened by atypical time gaps around the first post-cutoff interaction.
The choice of splitting protocol created unstable rankings across models on most evaluated datasets, demonstrating that evaluation protocol can affect conclusions about which system performs best.

Validation constructed with a matching global temporal split generally aligned most strongly with GTS test performance; for GTS Last, GT Last validation had the highest correlations on five of eight datasets.

At the q0.9 temporal cutoff, GTS retained a realistic future test interval but covered substantially fewer test users than LOO, illustrating a trade-off among recency, test duration, training volume, and statistical sample size.

Retraining selected models on combined training and validation data was particularly beneficial for global-temporal and user-based validation configurations and usually preserved the relative model-selection conclusions.

limitations: The experiments are offline evaluations and do not directly validate which split best predicts actual online production performance.
Only eight datasets and a limited collection of recommender architectures were experimentally compared, so ranking behavior can differ for other domains and model families.
Selecting a GTS cutoff remains dataset-dependent because user count, holdout duration, sequence length, and available training data trade off against one another.
Successive evaluation is computationally expensive for long holdout sequences, whereas Random targeting introduces stochasticity unless sampled targets or seeds are preserved.

The work studies temporal evaluation of recommender interactions rather than longitudinal workplace work-item states, cross-thread briefing, resolved or superseded state transitions, or omission/repetition of generated briefings.
raw_claims: Leave-one-out preserves each user's local ordering but can train on interactions that occur after another user's test interaction.
Global temporal splitting separates training from a later evaluation period and therefore avoids this form of future leakage.
The experiments used eight publicly available real-world recommendation datasets.
The paper evaluated HR, MRR, and NDCG without sampled negative-item evaluation.
GTS Random correlated most strongly with the Successive target across the aggregated comparisons.
GTS Last was also substantially more consistent with Successive evaluation than LOO in the aggregated results.
The All target had the weakest aggregate correlation with the Successive next-item evaluation.
Changing the split or GTS target could reorder recommender models.
Global-temporal validation generally produced the most reliable correspondence between validation and GTS test performance.
The Successive scheme most closely represents repeated next-item prediction after a temporal cutoff but costs more inference computation.
Random targeting requires control of random seeds or preservation of sampled targets for reproducibility.

analyses.title: Confidence guides spontaneous cognitive offloading
analyses.research_question: Does confidence in unaided prospective-memory ability guide people's use of external reminders even when the reminder strategy must be generated spontaneously rather than explicitly instructed?
analyses.methodology: The study recruited 435 US-based MTurk participants, with 363 datasets retained for analysis and participants assigned to an instructed-offloading group or a spontaneous-offloading group. In Phase 1 participants performed a delayed-intention task without offloading, whereas Phase 2 permitted rearranging target circles as external reminders; only the instructed group was explicitly told about this strategy. The authors measured prospective and retrospective confidence, objective task performance, reminder use, and questionnaire measures, and analysed the data using ANOVAs, t tests, Bayes factors, regression/path analyses, and additional robustness tests.

key_findings.finding: Participants who were never explicitly taught the reminder strategy nevertheless spontaneously used it, although their mean offloading rate was lower than that of participants who had been instructed about it.
Allowing offloading improved delayed-intention performance in both groups, with average hit rate increasing from Phase 1 to Phase 2.

Lower confidence in unaided Phase 1 performance predicted greater Phase 2 offloading in both the instructed and spontaneous groups, even when objective Phase 1 performance was included as a predictor.
key_findings.section: Results: Do metacognitive beliefs guide the use of compensatory strategies?

key_findings.finding: A general claim that objective memory ability robustly determines reminder use was not supported across groups; objective performance showed a negative relationship with offloading in the spontaneous group but not in the instructed group.
Participants updated later confidence partly on the basis of earlier task performance, indicating some adaptation of metacognitive estimates from experience.
key_findings.section: Results: Do metacognitive beliefs guide the use of compensatory strategies?

key_findings.finding: Most participants showed relatively stable reminder-use strategies across trials, despite group-level differences in how offloading changed over time.

limitations: The cover story made object movement permissible but may still have caused some participants who discovered the strategy to avoid using it, potentially underestimating spontaneous offloading.
The experimental reminder mechanism captures only one form of offloading, whereas real users can employ heterogeneous internal and external strategies.
The task was a controlled web experiment with US-based MTurk participants rather than a naturalistic longitudinal workplace setting.
The study examines delayed intentions over a short experiment and does not model explicit new, open, resolved, or superseded work-item states across briefing cycles.
It does not evaluate omission or repetition in generated workplace briefings.
raw_claims: Participants were divided into instructed and spontaneous offloading groups.
Both groups first completed a baseline phase in which delayed intentions had to be remembered without the experimental reminder strategy.
During the second phase, participants could move target circles to locations that served as external reminders.
The spontaneous group used reminders without receiving explicit instructions to do so.
The instructed group used the reminder strategy more frequently than the spontaneous group.
Task performance improved when offloading became possible.
Lower baseline confidence predicted more subsequent reminder use in both groups.
The confidence effect remained after accounting for objective baseline performance.
Participants showed meaningful correspondence between confidence judgements and their performance.
The authors made the study datasets and analysis scripts available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.

analyses.title: Supporting Prospective Information in Email
analyses.research_question: How do people use email to manage future actions and time-sensitive information, what deficiencies in email interfaces hinder this prospective-memory function, and how do these practices vary with users' organizational habits?
analyses.methodology: Twenty-two participants completed an online questionnaire about email use, and 19 of them also participated in in-person interviews that were audio-recorded and transcribed. The sample consisted mainly of researchers, student interns, and computer scientists, with an average of about ten years of email experience and self-reported receipt of roughly 25–50 messages per day. The study examined practices for retaining, monitoring, transferring, and deleting time-sensitive messages and used descriptive counts and non-parametric association tests such as Somers' d to relate prospective-email practices to broader organizational behavior.

key_findings.finding: Fifteen of the 19 interviewed participants retained prospective messages in their inbox, showing that the inbox commonly served as storage for information about future actions and events.
Fifteen of 19 interviewees also used email as a reminder mechanism for email-related actions, other tasks, or future events.
Managing prospective information often required repeated inbox review or other manual techniques for keeping actionable messages salient, creating substantial monitoring and scanning overhead.

Participants who retained prospective messages in email also tended to search or consult email more often outside the immediate context of replying or composing, consistent with active monitoring of pending information.

Prospective-email practices were statistically associated with other organizational habits, supporting the argument that tools for pending information should accommodate different user styles rather than assume one universal workflow.

Conventional email captured that a future intention existed but poorly represented the action details, execution context, timing, event organization, and later retrieval needed to support prospective memory.

limitations: The study is small, with only 22 questionnaire respondents and 19 interviewees.
The participant population was heavily weighted toward researchers, interns, and computer scientists, limiting generalizability to broader workplace populations.
The evidence is based primarily on questionnaire and interview reports rather than instrumented longitudinal email behavior.
The study identifies design deficiencies but does not experimentally evaluate a production intervention for tracking prospective information.
The work predates modern threaded, mobile, collaborative, and AI-assisted communication environments.
It does not explicitly represent work-item transitions such as new, open, resolved, or superseded, nor does it measure briefing omission or repetition.
raw_claims: The study surveyed 22 email users and interviewed 19 of them in person.
Most participants in the sample were computer scientists.
Participants reported substantial prior experience with email and regular daily message traffic.
Fifteen of the 19 interviewees kept messages concerning future actions or events in their inbox.
Fifteen of the 19 interviewees used email as a reminder environment.
Users often had to rescan the inbox to keep track of pending information.
Some users manually manipulated message position or forwarded messages to themselves to keep tasks visible.
Keeping prospective messages was associated with more frequent information lookup in email outside composing and replying.
Prospective-message handling was related to participants' broader organizational habits.
Existing email interfaces did not explicitly record important action, context, and timing information for future intentions.
The paper argues that support for prospective memory should become an explicit email-design concern.

analyses.title: Strategic reminder setting for time-based intentions: Influence of metacognition, delay length, and cue visibility
analyses.research_question: How do delay length, metacognitive beliefs, and access to a visible time cue influence strategic reminder setting and performance for time-based prospective-memory intentions?
analyses.methodology: Experiment 1 used a preregistered within-subject 3-by-2 design with 52 Prolific participants, manipulating 10-, 20-, and 30-second delays and unaided versus reminder conditions while participants concurrently performed a two-back task with a visible clock. Experiment 2 used a preregistered 3-by-2-by-2 design with a final sample of 96 participants, adding a between-subject manipulation in which the clock was either continuously visible or had to be deliberately revealed. Participants made prospective and retrospective confidence judgements, and the authors analysed prospective-memory accuracy, false alarms, misses, reminder use, clock checking, metacognitive bias, and ongoing-task performance using ANOVA, correlations, and regression models in R.

key_findings.finding: Longer delays reduced first-response prospective-memory accuracy, lowered confidence, and substantially increased reminder use.
key_findings.section: Experiment 1 Results: Effect of delay length

key_findings.finding: Setting reminders improved prospective-memory performance, reduced errors, and produced larger benefits at longer delays in both experiments.
key_findings.section: Experiment 1 PM performance improvement; Experiment 2 PM performance improvement

key_findings.finding: Within participants, a steeper decline in confidence as delay increased predicted a steeper rise in reminder use, even though the confidence decline did not track the corresponding decline in objective unaided accuracy.
key_findings.section: Experiment 1 Metacognitive judgement and reminder usage; General Discussion

key_findings.finding: The preregistered hypothesis that people with lower average confidence across participants would generally use more reminders was not consistently supported; mean confidence did not significantly predict overall reminder use in the main analyses.
key_findings.section: Experiments 1 and 2: Metacognitive judgement and reminder usage

key_findings.finding: Participants used significantly more reminders when the clock was hidden than when it remained visible, and clock visibility explained reminder usage independently of average confidence in Experiment 2.
key_findings.section: Experiment 2 Reminder usage and General Discussion

key_findings.finding: Unaided prospective-memory accuracy did not significantly differ between visible- and hidden-clock groups, but hiding the clock imposed a measurable cost on the concurrent two-back task.
key_findings.section: Experiment 2 PM performance and General Discussion: Time monitoring behaviour

key_findings.finding: Among hidden-clock participants, more frequent deliberate clock checking was associated with better unaided prospective-memory accuracy.
Objective performance differences did not reliably drive reminder allocation across delay conditions, indicating that strategic offloading followed perceived need more closely than measured need.

limitations: The maximum intention delay was only 30 seconds, whereas many everyday and workplace intentions persist for minutes, hours, or days.
Participants were instructed to prioritize the ongoing two-back task, and reminder strategies might differ when the prospective task has higher priority.
The controlled online task does not establish that the same reminder-allocation behavior occurs in naturalistic workplace environments.
Experiment 2 excluded participants who never used reminders, which narrows conclusions about population-level differences in reminder propensity.
Several informative analyses were exploratory or non-preregistered and therefore require greater caution than the primary preregistered tests.
The study addresses individual time-based intentions rather than explicit longitudinal work-item state transitions, cross-thread aggregation, or omission/repetition in briefings.
raw_claims: Experiment 1 compared 10-, 20-, and 30-second intentions under unaided and reminder conditions.
Experiment 2 additionally compared a continuously visible clock with a clock that participants had to reveal manually.
Participants became less confident as intention delays increased.
Reminder use increased as delays became longer.
External reminders improved prospective-memory accuracy and reduced errors.
The reminder benefit was generally larger at longer delays.
The within-person change in confidence across delays predicted the within-person change in reminder use.
Average confidence across individuals did not consistently predict how many reminders they used.
Participants used more reminders when the clock was hidden.
Hiding the clock did not significantly reduce unaided prospective-memory accuracy but increased demands on the concurrent task.
More frequent clock checking in the hidden-clock condition was associated with better unaided prospective-memory performance.
The experiments and analysis plans were preregistered.
Data and analysis code for both experiments were made available through OSF.
